attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The revision restores 'entirely dependent', 'largely based on' and the 'want to and are able to' pairing. It is a causal-dependence claim, not a forecast that the labs will spend $400B.

contract.note: Reading growth as revenue and treating $400B as combined lab compute spending are ordinary readings. 'Largely', the set of large companies and the window are undefined, so the result turns on the evaluator's interpretation.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's 10-Q shows revenue concentrated among a few direct and indirect customers. It does not trace that demand to the two labs or explain why buyers invest.

Meta's own disclosure cites its own training, inference and core business as uses, which suggests a demand driver separate from the labs. It is unquantified and self-reported, so it cannot establish an independent path.

reviews.rationale: Proving the claim requires showing that NVIDIA's growth depends entirely on big-company spending, and that expectations about lab spending mainly drive that spending. The packet shows customer concentration and one buyer citing its own uses (Meta), but has no customer-level attribution, no record of buyers' investment decisions, and no counterfactual. It neither establishes nor refutes the dependence.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Despite its AI capex' is a slight addition, but it is implied by the surrounding capex passage. The comparative 'far worse' is dropped and cannot be measured anyway. The core claim, that Meta has no real AI business, is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'AI business' as substantive commercial sales of AI products, beyond internal ad improvements, is an ordinary reading and fits his 'nothing to do with AI' framing. But 'really' sets no materiality threshold, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Meta's 10-Q, reproduced in an exchange-hosted document, says AI-glasses sales rose in the quarter. Reality Labs revenue grew only $61M in total, and glasses sales are not broken out. That shows the activity exists but not its substance, so it does not meet the contract's contradiction bar.
The earnings call mentions a recently launched, priced model API. It gives no launch date within the quarter and no revenue.

reviews.rationale: Meta had some customer-facing AI products in Q2 2026: AI-glasses sales and possibly an API. That argues against a total absence of an AI business, but the scale is unquantified and appears small, and the contract says a minor, unquantified revenue stream does not settle 'really'. The packet does not establish whether Meta had a substantive AI business in the quarter.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. He frames the excerpt as his own earlier premium piece ('per last premium') and endorses it here.

semantics.note: The proposition combines 'contracting' with the receivables-concentration support he gives right after it. That is a fair rendering of the passage.

contract.note: Reading 'contracting' as fewer customers is ordinary and fair, and it asks for a like-for-like concentration check. But the result does depend on interpretation: read as concentration, the like-for-like data contradict it; read as customer count, there is no data. The contract's 'false' flag on interpretation_determines_result is wrong.

evidence.note: The Q2 10-Q gives five direct-customer receivables shares summing to 70%, confirming that figure. The top three sum to 49%, not the 44% he cited. No customer counts are given.

In Q1 the top three held 64% of receivables. Against Q2's 49%, like-for-like top-three concentration fell by 15 points, and five customers rather than three now exceed 10%. This contradicts the 'increasingly concentrated' part.

reviews.rationale: The 70% top-five figure checks out. But comparing top three with top three, receivables concentration fell from 64% to 49% between Q1 and Q2, which contradicts the supporting trend. The core claim, a shrinking customer base, needs comparable customer counts, and the packet has none. The contract says falling concentration alone does not settle counts, so the core claim is unresolved even though its concentration support fails.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: Firm 'will', conditional on stopping. The proposition keeps the antecedent and the 'cannot stop' inference. It drops 'the second', but the contract restores the immediacy.

contract.note: Treating 'stop' as full cessation and 'the second' as the first investor discussion are ordinary readings. The contract rightly keeps the claim that they 'cannot stop' separate from the investor-response forecast.

evidence.note: Microsoft's earnings-call transcript, a company disclosure reproduced by a third party, reports $45.2B of capex in the September quarter, so Microsoft did not stop. That is total capex, and it says nothing of Google or Amazon. The antecedent is not triggered.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast with no deadline. The packet shows no named company stopping AI capex; Microsoft kept spending, so the antecedent has not occurred. Under policy the conditional is not scored, and no conclusive event exists.
